title: How Trump Put Jensen Huang Back in Charge of Nvidia

For days, Nvidia shareholders clamored for Jensen Huang to return to the company, as did thousands of its employees and a broad array of Silicon Valley luminaries. In the end, though, it was President Donald Trump who set the stage for one of the most remarkable CEO comebacks in tech history.

The president played a critical role in the Nvidia board’s head-spinning announcement Monday morning that it had unanimously reinstated Huang as CEO, according to a person familiar with the matter and Trump himself. Over the weekend, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told the president that the department had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Huang, according to a Justice Department official. title: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate
summary:
Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done—Anthropic and SpaceX—only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. 

That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year—including OpenAI—but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. 

In that context, it’s a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are dominating.

summary:
Between November 12 and 17, at least eight American systems failed. Microsoft 365 went down, in part because of a latent software bug dating from July. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop after a flood of network traffic destabilized aging equipment. Chase customers lost access to online banking. The National Security Agency’s classified network faltered during routine maintenance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the failures were unrelated and that there was “zero evidence” any adversary caused them. That may be right; it is beside the point. In every case explained so far, the cause lay inside the system: a flaw it already carried, equipment it had outgrown, or the work of keeping it running.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Quantum Computing, and the Future of Digital Security
summary:
Introduction: Two Revolutions on a Collision Course

Two technologies are changing the world at the same time. Artificial intelligence is already having a significant effect on business, science, intelligence, and military operations. Quantum computing is not nearly as mature, but it has the potential to change how we solve some very difficult problems. One of those problems is the mathematics on which much of our digital security depends.

We generally discuss these technologies separately. That makes sense from a scientific standpoint, but not necessarily from a security standpoint. Their intersection could change both the nature of cyber threats and the amount of time we have to prepare for them.

Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia, with the board announcing his restatement as CEO on Monday morning. He was gone for just 11 days, initially resigning as CEO on Nov. 12 after acknowledging an affair with a woman who U.S. authorities think might’ve been a Chinese spy. His relationship with the woman goes back years, part of Nvidia’s deep network in Asia that has allowed its chips to end up in the hands of Chinese companies. Huang has advocated against America’s chip export ban and struck a deep relationship with President Donald Trump, who was a major force in convincing Nvidia’s board to rehire Huang. The intertwined scandals and drama around Huang and Nvidia has roiled the broader stock market, exacerbating fears about the AI economy.  At one point, Nvidia’s stock had been nearly halved from its recent high.

title: How Amazon Plays the Long, Expensive Data Center Game That Neoclouds Can’t
summary:
INDIANA, Penn.—A visit this week to an Amazon data center project in Pennsylvania coal country gave me a glimpse of the era we all knew was coming: when tech giants lay claim to some of the hardest-to-secure AI infrastructure while smaller cloud providers, which Nvidia has propped up financially, are trying to hang on.

The 4.4-gigawatt campus in Pennsylvania, once home to a 2-GW coal-fired power plant near the economically depressed borough of Homer City, could become one of the largest AI power parks in the country.

Few companies can marshal the resources as readily as Amazon to transform the site from what it was—a Rust Belt relic that once employed thousands of people but released coal dust and arsenic—into an Appalachian hilltop of gas-fired electrons flowing into 36 buildings powering the AI of Anthropic or others.

title: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
summary:
What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful

I’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.

Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)

The decline is costing colleges millions in tuition revenue and depriving American students of the cultural benefits of international classmates

Until 2025, students from Brazil, Nigeria, Thailand, Turkey, Turkmenistan and Zambia eagerly accepted a full scholarship to attend Indiana University in Bloomington, a town in the midwestern United States where fans are passionate about the Hoosiers – the school’s basketball and football teams.

The town also hosts the Little 500, a famous bicycle race that can attract more than 25,000 people. And most importantly for prospective students, the school has well-regarded academic programs.
